correctness.rationale: Support-width additivity, ordered-coordinate cut decomposition, a strict triangle-equality characterization, and exact split tube counting reduce all widths to two-level cuts. The full finite interval \(4\le n\le63\) is certified by 750605 exact integer comparisons across 1830 parameter profiles, including equality cases; for \(n\ge64\), a uniform analytical comparison against B/sqrt(floor(n^2/4)) excludes every noncentral cut. The remaining central cut minimization is strictly convex in the independent-class count (discrete exponential sum). The replayed standalone checker also verifies 392 symbolic crossing identities by direct tube enumeration.

evidence: The complete-graph case has all nonempty subsets as tubes; the complete split graph excludes nonsingleton independent-only subsets, so the complete-graph formula does not imply its Euclidean width.
The biclique has tubes meeting both color classes plus singletons; genuine split graph tubes include all clique-containing subsets and differ from biclique tubes.
The stellohedron is the clique-size-one boundary, excluded here. General normal-fan or deformation-cone descriptions specify no scale-invariant width value for the selected Minkowski realization.
broader_coverage.reasoning: Related same-threshold results cover neither every \(c,m\ge2\) split profile nor the simultaneous class/total bisection classification. A generic crossing-count reduction is reusable, but computing the global minimum over the split tube system and proving its parameter-uniform phase change requires the new comparison and certificate.

value.rationale: Complete split graph associahedra are a well-motivated two-parameter family interpolating between star and complete graph cases, but their exact Euclidean minimum width is not determined by known skeleton diameters. The theorem gives a complete, arbitrary-class-size metric invariant, a universal and sharp 15-vertex change of all minimizing normals independent of the clique ratio, and a precise census of their simultaneous clique/independent balancing. This is more than a renamed boundary-family or single numerical gain.
